parts:
Hi Yves and folks,

Thanks for all the help provided for my question in earlier threads, already. However I don't have a secure solution to the following "problem".

I am running a CFA with only dichotomous, ordered IVs/exogenous variables with approx 30% missings which are distributed completely at random. As I found multiple ways of dealing with these and all models I tried converge and make sense, I am still unsure which is (most?) correct or super-wrong. I'd be glad if you could find a second for a vote (or a better alternative):

1. estimator WLSMV and missing = pariwise (without specifying which variables are ordered)
2. not specifying the estimator and specifying what variables are ordered and missing = fiml (although I thought that shouldn't work, as fiml would be in need for MLx, but it did)
3. estimator MLR and missing = fiml (which due to the nature of the data isn't correct, but works best re fit/loadings)

Any other ideas?

Thanks!

parts: I am running a CFA with only dichotomous, ordered IVs/exogenous variables
Do you mean endogenous?  Indicators are outcomes, not predictors.
with approx 30% missings which are distributed completely at random.
If this is a MIMIC model where you are predicting the latent variable with categorical predictors, you could treat "NA" as a category.

As I found multiple ways of dealing with these and all models I tried converge and make sense, I am still unsure which is (most?) correct or super-wrong. I'd be glad if you could find a second for a vote (or a better alternative):

1. estimator WLSMV and missing = pariwise (without specifying which variables are ordered)

So your binary variables are the indicators?  Then this is probably your best available option, if the data are truly MCAR (how can you be sure?).  If they are MAR and you have relevant auxiliary variables, multiple imputation would be better.  That would be facilitated using the run() function in the semTools package.

2. not specifying the estimator and specifying what variables are ordered and missing = fiml (although I thought that shouldn't work, as fiml would be in need for MLx, but it did)
3. estimator MLR and missing = fiml (which due to the nature of the data isn't correct, but works best re fit/loadings)

What do you mean "works best"?  The best answer is the right one, not the most convenient one.  MLR does not yield unbiased estimates of factor loadings unless ordered indicators have at least 7 categories:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen

parts: when I change class to ("ordered" "factor"), I don't get robust SEs (basically no robust anything)

I think you are mistaken.  lavaan provides robust SEs and test statistics by default when using DWLS estimation.  

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html  (read the bottom paragraph)

Does this return "standard" or something robust like "robust.huber.white" or "first.order"?

lavInspect(fit, "options")$se
and the "not positive definite" error (with some not really tiny negative eigenvalues

Which matrix was NPD?  If it just a Heywood case in the parameter matrices, it should be a warning, not an error (i.e., you still get results, but you should inspect the source of NPD-ness so you can see whether it is really a problem).
Should I a) still use this version (as the factor loadings e.g., make much sense still) or b) keep the class as "numeric" (shoudn't WLSMV take care of that?)?

You have dichotomous variables, so MLE is not appropriate.  MML is the only likelihood-based estimator that would be (i.e., an IRT model).  You need to set their class to "ordered" in the data.frame, or tell lavaan which variables are ordered in the call to the function.  If you have an NPD parameter matrix, you can still consider your solution acceptable if the CI around the Heywood case includes plausible boundaries (e.g., if the CI around a variance includes positive values, or the CI around a correlation includes values within +/- 1; you may need to transform the limits around a covariance estimate into correlations to test that).

http://smr.sagepub.com/content/41/1/124.short

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
